topic: Slow Dependencies Bleed Gateway Threads Into Full Outage
postText:
One slow upstream dependency is more lethal than an outright dead one.

A dead service fails fast with connection resets in milliseconds. A hung service keeps client sockets open, holds gateway threads hostage, and slowly exhausts system file descriptors until your edge collapses.

In our healthcare IT environment, edge gateways mediate everything from EHR pipelines to third-party insurance lookups. During peak triage, an external insurance verification service degraded from 120ms to 28s response times. Our gateway kept accepting connections, queuing incoming requests, and stacking thread pools. Within two minutes, all HTTP worker threads were occupied waiting on unresponsive remote sockets. Result: internal emergency orders couldn't pass through because third-party billing choked the gateway.

We stopped the bleeding using three defensive patterns:
1. Edge Token-Bucket Limiting: Cap concurrent inbound requests per client identity and route before they hit reverse proxy buffers.
2. Circuit Breakers: Wrap brittle endpoints with sliding-window circuit breakers. If latency exceeds 2s or error rates hit 25%, trip open immediately and serve graceful cached defaults.
3. Bulkheading: Isolate thread pools per upstream service. Degraded billing integrations can exhaust their own dedicated worker pool without touching clinic or lab telemetry routes.

How do you calibrate your circuit breaker error thresholds in production to avoid flapping while protecting edge connection pools?
